question: According to the Wyoming CDL Manual, how much more likely are fully loaded combination rigs to roll over in a crash compared to empty rigs?
choice_a: Ten times more likely
choice_b: Twice as likely
choice_c: Five times more likely
choice_d: They are equally likely to roll over
explanation: The manual states fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: Which two practices does the manual identify as helping prevent rollover in a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Driving fast around turns and raising the cargo's center of gravity
choice_b: Keeping cargo as close to the ground as possible and driving slowly around turns
choice_c: Using the trailer hand valve and braking hard into curves
choice_d: Loading cargo to one side and increasing following distance
explanation: The manual says keeping cargo low and driving slowly around turns are the two things that help prevent rollover.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: What is the technical term the manual uses for the effect that causes a trailer to overturn during a quick lane change (the 'crack-the-whip' effect)?
choice_a: Off-tracking
choice_b: Trailer jackknife
choice_c: Rearward amplification
choice_d: Cargo shift
explanation: The manual explains that 'rearward amplification' causes the crack-the-whip effect during a quick lane change.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: Per Figure 6.1 in the manual, what is the rearward amplification of triples with 27-ft trailers, meaning how much more easily the last trailer can roll over compared to a five-axle tractor-semitrailer?
choice_a: 1.0 times as easily
choice_b: 2.0 times as easily
choice_c: 3.0 times as easily
choice_d: 3.5 times as easily
explanation: The manual states triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5, meaning you can roll the last trailer of triples 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor-semitrailer.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: What following-distance rule does the manual give for combination vehicles?
choice_a: At least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph
choice_b: A fixed 4 seconds regardless of vehicle length or speed
choice_c: One second for each 20 feet of vehicle length only
choice_d: Two car lengths per 10 mph of speed
explanation: The manual instructs following at least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second when going over 40 mph.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: According to the manual, how do bobtail tractors (tractors without semitrailers) compare to a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight when stopping?
choice_a: Bobtails stop more smoothly and in a shorter distance
choice_b: Bobtails can be very hard to stop smoothly and take longer to stop
choice_c: There is no difference in stopping ability
choice_d: Bobtails stop faster but less smoothly
explanation: The manual warns that tests show bobtails can be very hard to stop smoothly, taking longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.3 Brake Early

question: Why does the manual warn that large combination vehicles can take longer to stop when empty than when fully loaded?
choice_a: Empty trailers have no brakes at all
choice_b: Empty trailers have less air pressure available
choice_c: Lightly loaded vehicles have very stiff springs and strong brakes that give poor traction, making it easy to lock up the wheels
choice_d: Empty trailers always exceed the speed limit
explanation: The manual explains that when lightly loaded, the very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and make it easy to lock up the wheels.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.3 Brake Early

question: Which types of trailers does the manual warn are most likely to get stuck on raised railroad-highway crossings?
choice_a: Flatbed trailers and tankers
choice_b: Refrigerated vans and dry vans
choice_c: Double trailers with tandem axles
choice_d: Low slung units (lowboy, car carrier, possum-belly livestock trailer) and a single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor
explanation: The manual lists low slung units and single-axle tractors pulling long trailers with landing gear set for tandem-axle tractors as units that can get stuck on raised crossings.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.4 Railroad-highway Crossings

question: If your combination vehicle becomes stuck on railroad tracks, what does the manual instruct you to do?
choice_a: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or the emergency number posted at the crossing, giving the location using identifiable landmarks such as the DOT number
choice_b: Stay in the vehicle and try to rock it free
choice_c: Immediately apply the trailer hand valve to hold position
choice_d: Wait for the train to pass before taking any action
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to get out and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number using landmarks such as the DOT number to identify the crossing location.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.4 Railroad-highway Crossings

question: According to the manual, what is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel pull sharply
choice_b: Seeing it in your mirrors, especially after applying the brakes hard
choice_c: Hearing the ABS warning lamp buzzer
choice_d: Noticing a drop in the air pressure gauge
explanation: The manual says the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors, and to check the mirrors any time you brake hard.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What does the manual say you should do to stop a trailer skid once you recognize it?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand valve firmly to straighten out the rig
choice_b: Accelerate to regain traction
choice_c: Release the brakes to get traction back; do not use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out the rig
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel sharply into the skid
explanation: The manual instructs releasing the brakes to regain traction and specifically warns against using the trailer hand brake to straighten out a jackknifing trailer, since the trailer brakes caused the skid.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: The manual states a 'trailer jackknife' (where the trailer swings around after its wheels lock up) is more likely to happen when the trailer is:
choice_a: Fully loaded with cargo centered
choice_b: Carrying hazardous materials
choice_c: Coupled to a converter dolly
choice_d: Empty or lightly loaded
explanation: The manual states this type of skid is more likely to happen when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: How does the manual define 'offtracking' (also called 'cheating')?
choice_a: The rear wheels of a vehicle following a different path than the front wheels when going around a corner
choice_b: The trailer swinging out after the brakes lock up
choice_c: The tractor and trailer separating unexpectedly
choice_d: The cargo shifting to one side of the trailer
explanation: The manual defines offtracking as the rear wheels following a different path than the front wheels when a vehicle goes around a corner.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: According to the manual, which part of a combination vehicle offtracks the most in a turn?
choice_a: The front wheels of the tractor
choice_b: The rear wheels of the last trailer, if there is more than one trailer
choice_c: The rear wheels of the powered unit only
choice_d: All wheels offtrack the same amount
explanation: The manual states that if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will offtrack the most.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: Per Figure 6.4 in the manual, which turning technique is correct when a combination vehicle cannot complete a turn without entering another lane?
choice_a: The 'jug handle' technique, swinging wide to the left before starting the turn
choice_b: Straddling both lanes throughout the turn
choice_c: The 'button hook' technique — turning wide as you complete the turn rather than swinging wide before starting it
choice_d: Stopping mid-turn to let following traffic pass
explanation: Figure 6.4 labels the 'jug handle' approach as INCORRECT and the 'button hook' — turning wide as you complete the turn — as CORRECT, since it keeps other drivers from passing on the right.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: When backing up a vehicle that is pulling a trailer, how does the manual say you should turn the steering wheel, compared to backing a car, straight truck, or bus?
choice_a: The same direction you want the trailer to go, exactly as with a car
choice_b: It doesn't matter which direction as long as you go slowly
choice_c: Only counterclockwise, regardless of desired direction
choice_d: In the opposite direction from backing a car — turn the wheel opposite the direction you want the trailer to go
explanation: The manual states that when backing a trailer, you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from how you would turn it backing a car, straight truck, or bus.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: If you must back a trailer on a curved path, to which side does the manual recommend backing so you can see?
choice_a: The driver's side
choice_b: The passenger's side
choice_c: Either side, it makes no difference
choice_d: Directly backward using only mirrors on the passenger side
explanation: The manual instructs that if you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: According to the manual, how should you correct a trailer's drift immediately while backing?
choice_a: Pull forward completely and start over every time
choice_b: Turn the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift
choice_c: Apply the trailer hand valve
choice_d: Turn the top of the steering wheel opposite the direction of the drift
explanation: The manual says to correct drift by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift as soon as you see the trailer getting off the proper path.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: What does the manual recommend if you need to reposition your vehicle while backing a trailer?
choice_a: Never stop until backing is complete
choice_b: Exit the vehicle and push the trailer by hand
choice_c: Make pull-ups — pull forward to re-position your vehicle as needed
choice_d: Use the trailer hand valve to reposition
explanation: The manual instructs making pull-ups (pulling forward) to re-position the vehicle as needed when backing a trailer.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: What is the trailer hand valve also called, and what does the manual say it should be used for?
choice_a: The Johnson bar; used for normal everyday braking
choice_b: The trolley valve; used only for parking the trailer
choice_c: The relay valve; used to charge the trailer air tanks
choice_d: The trolley valve or Johnson bar; it should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not for driving
explanation: The manual identifies the trailer hand valve as the trolley valve or Johnson bar and states it should be used only to test the trailer brakes because of the danger of causing a skid.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why does the manual say you should never use the trailer hand valve for parking?
choice_a: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes in trailers that don't have spring brakes
choice_b: It wears out the brake shoes faster than the parking brake
choice_c: It is illegal in Wyoming to use the hand valve while parked
choice_d: It only works when the engine is running
explanation: The manual warns that all the air might leak out and unlock the brakes in trailers without spring brakes if the hand valve is used for parking; always use the parking brakes instead.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: What is the function of the tractor protection valve described in the manual?
choice_a: It controls the trailer's electrical lighting circuit
choice_b: It keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak
choice_c: It regulates engine RPM during downhill braking
choice_d: It locks the fifth wheel automatically
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve

question: At what air pressure range does the manual say the tractor protection valve will close automatically?
choice_a: 5 to 10 psi
choice_b: 50 to 70 psi
choice_c: 20 to 45 psi
choice_d: 100 to 120 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve

question: How does the manual describe the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles?
choice_a: A blue round knob you pull to supply air
choice_b: A green square button you push to shut off air
choice_c: A yellow triangular lever with only one position
choice_d: A red eight-sided knob — push it in to supply the trailer with air, pull it out to shut the air off and apply the trailer emergency brakes
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as a red eight-sided knob, pushed in to supply air and pulled out to shut it off and apply the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.3 Trailer Air Supply Control

question: On older vehicles without an automatic air supply knob, what does the manual say may be used instead, and what are its two positions called?
choice_a: A lever with 'normal' and 'emergency' positions
choice_b: A foot pedal with 'on' and 'off' positions
choice_c: A rotary dial with 'low' and 'high' positions
choice_d: A hand crank with 'open' and 'closed' positions
explanation: The manual states older vehicles may have a lever rather than a knob, with a 'normal' position for pulling a trailer and an 'emergency' position to shut off air and set the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.3 Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What does the manual say the service air line (also called the control or signal line) does?
choice_a: Supplies air to fill the trailer air tanks only
choice_b: Carries air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand valve, with pressure that changes depending on how hard the brake is applied
choice_c: Controls the emergency brakes only
choice_d: Powers the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual explains the service line carries air controlled by the foot brake or hand valve, with pressure changing depending on how hard the brake is applied.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.4 Trailer Air Lines

question: According to the manual, what are the two purposes of the emergency air line (also called the supply line)?
choice_a: To power the trailer lights and to cool the brakes
choice_b: To carry cargo data and to charge the batteries
choice_c: To supply air to the trailer air tanks and to control the emergency brakes on combination vehicles
choice_d: To operate the ABS system and to inflate the tires
explanation: The manual states the emergency line has two purposes: supplying air to the trailer air tanks and controlling the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.4 Trailer Air Lines

question: What color coding does the manual describe for the service and emergency air lines?
choice_a: Service lines are green; emergency lines are yellow
choice_b: Service lines are black; emergency lines are white
choice_c: Service lines are orange; emergency lines are purple
choice_d: Service lines are blue; emergency (supply) lines are red
explanation: The manual states blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines to help avoid mixing them up.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: How does the manual say you should connect glad hands (hose couplers)?
choice_a: Press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90-degree angle to each other, then turn the glad hand to join and lock the couplers
choice_b: Snap them together at a 45-degree angle without turning
choice_c: Screw them together using a wrench for a tight seal
choice_d: Align them parallel and slide them straight into place
explanation: The manual instructs pressing the two seals together with the couplers at a 90-degree angle, then turning the glad hand attached to the hose to join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What happens, according to the manual, if you cross the air lines when coupling?
choice_a: Nothing; the system automatically corrects crossed lines
choice_b: Supply air is sent to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so spring brakes won't release
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp turns off
choice_d: The tractor protection valve locks permanently open
explanation: The manual warns that crossing the air lines sends supply air to the service line instead of charging the trailer tanks, so air won't be available to release the trailer spring brakes.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What is the purpose of the 'dead end' or dummy couplers mentioned in the manual?
choice_a: To supply backup air pressure in an emergency
choice_b: To provide a secondary electrical connection
choice_c: To keep water and dirt out of the coupler and air lines when hoses are not attached to a trailer
choice_d: To automatically test the trailer brakes
explanation: The manual states dummy couplers, used when the air lines are not connected to a trailer, prevent water and dirt from getting into the coupler and air lines.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: According to the manual, what do trailer air tanks do?
choice_a: Store fuel for the auxiliary power unit
choice_b: Cool the tractor protection valve
choice_c: Store cargo securement straps
choice_d: Provide the air pressure used to operate trailer brakes, filled by the emergency (supply) line from the tractor
explanation: The manual states trailer air tanks are filled by the emergency (supply) line from the tractor and provide the air pressure used to operate the trailer brakes.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.6 Trailer Air Tanks

question: Why does the manual say you should drain each air tank every day, even if the tanks have automatic drains?
choice_a: To make sure water and oil don't build up and cause the brakes to work incorrectly
choice_b: To reduce total vehicle weight before weigh stations
choice_c: To prevent the ABS malfunction lamp from illuminating
choice_d: Draining is only required once a month, not daily
explanation: The manual explains that water and oil buildup can keep brakes from working correctly, so each tank should be drained every day even if it has an automatic drain.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.6 Trailer Air Tanks

question: According to the manual, where must shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) be open versus closed on a combination that tows multiple trailers?
choice_a: All shut-off valves must be closed except the ones on the first trailer
choice_b: All shut-off valves must be open except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed
choice_c: Shut-off valves are only found on the tractor, never on trailers
choice_d: All shut-off valves must remain closed at all times while driving
explanation: The manual states all shut-off valves must be in the open position, except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.7 Shut-off Valves

question: According to the manual, which combination-vehicle components are not required to have spring brakes, and what do they rely on instead?
choice_a: All modern trailers; they rely on the ABS system
choice_b: Only tractors; they rely on the trailer hand valve
choice_c: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975; they rely on emergency brakes powered by air stored in the trailer air tank
choice_d: Only doubles and triples; they rely on the parking brake alone
explanation: The manual states converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes and instead have emergency brakes that work from air stored in the trailer air tank.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.8 Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: When older trailer emergency brakes activate
question: The manual states that on trailers without spring brakes, the emergency brakes come on whenever:
choice_a: The foot brake is pressed lightly
choice_b: The ABS malfunction lamp illuminates
choice_c: The engine is turned off
choice_d: The air supply knob is pulled out or the trailer is disconnected
explanation: The manual states these trailers have no parking brake, and the emergency brakes come on whenever the air supply knob is pulled out or the trailer is disconnected.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.2.8 Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: Per the manual, which trailers and converter dollies are required to have ABS?
choice_a: Those built on or after March 1, 1998
choice_b: Those built on or after March 1, 1988
choice_c: All trailers regardless of build date
choice_d: Only trailers hauling hazardous materials
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: What does the manual say about the ABS malfunction lamp on trailers?
choice_a: It is red and located on the rear bumper only
choice_b: It is yellow and located on the left side, either the front or rear corner
choice_c: It is blue and mounted on the roof of the trailer
choice_d: It flashes only when the trailer is empty
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: According to the manual, when does ABS activate?
choice_a: Continuously, throughout every brake application
choice_b: Only when the parking brake is set
choice_c: Only when wheels are about to lock up; it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability
choice_d: Only above 55 mph
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to normal brakes that only activates when wheels are about to lock up, and it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten stopping distance, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, it always cuts stopping distance in half
choice_b: Yes, but only on wet pavement
choice_c: No, ABS eliminates the need for following distance
choice_d: No — ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
explanation: The manual states ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: If your ABS malfunctions, what does the manual instruct you to do?
choice_a: Drive normally using your regular brakes, but get the system serviced soon
choice_b: Immediately park the vehicle and refuse to move it
choice_c: Disable the regular brakes and rely on the parking brake
choice_d: Increase speed since ABS is no longer limiting you
explanation: The manual states that if your ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes, so you should drive normally but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: According to the manual, if only the trailer has ABS and you start a tractor jackknife or lose steering control, what should you do?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand valve immediately
choice_b: Let up on the brakes, if you can safely do so, until you gain control
choice_c: Press the brake pedal harder to activate the trailer ABS
choice_d: Pull the trailer air supply knob out
explanation: The manual states that when only the trailer has ABS, if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, you should let up on the brakes, if you can safely do so, until you gain control.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: As part of Step 1 (Inspect Fifth Wheel) when coupling a tractor-semitrailer, what does the manual say about the fifth wheel plate?
choice_a: It should be wiped completely dry of any lubricant
choice_b: It should be painted to prevent rust
choice_c: It should be greased as required; failure to lubricate it could cause steering problems from friction between tractor and trailer
choice_d: It should be replaced before every coupling
explanation: The manual states the fifth wheel plate must be greased as required, since failure to lubricate it could cause steering problems from friction between the tractor and trailer.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 1

question: Why does the manual warn against backing the tractor under the trailer at an angle (Step 3, Position Tractor)?
choice_a: It voids the CDL road test
choice_b: It causes the glad hands to disconnect
choice_c: It overheats the fifth wheel plate
choice_d: You might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
explanation: The manual warns never to back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 3

question: According to Step 6 (Check Trailer Height) of the coupling procedure, what problem can occur if the trailer is too low when the tractor backs under it?
choice_a: The tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose
choice_b: The kingpin will automatically eject
choice_c: The landing gear will retract on its own
choice_d: The service line will disconnect
explanation: The manual warns that if the trailer is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose (and if too high, it may not couple correctly).
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 6

topic: Locking trailer brakes before backing under
question: Before backing the tractor under the trailer (Step 9, Lock Trailer Brakes), what does the manual instruct you to do?
choice_a: Push in the air supply knob to release the trailer brakes
choice_b: Pull out the 'air supply' knob or move the tractor protection valve control from 'normal' to 'emergency'
choice_c: Disconnect both glad hands from the tractor
choice_d: Lower the landing gear fully
explanation: Step 9 instructs pulling out the air supply knob or moving the tractor protection valve control from 'normal' to 'emergency' to lock the trailer brakes before backing under.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 9

question: How does Step 11 (Check Connection for Security) say to verify the trailer is locked onto the tractor?
choice_a: Visually inspect from outside the cab only
choice_b: Sound the horn and listen for an echo
choice_c: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked
choice_d: Disconnect the air lines and check for a pressure drop
explanation: Step 11 instructs raising the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pulling the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 11

question: During Step 13 (Inspect Coupling), what should you check regarding the space between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: A wide visible space is normal and expected
choice_b: Space is only a concern if the trailer is loaded
choice_c: Space should only be checked after driving one mile
choice_d: There should be no space between upper and lower fifth wheel — space indicates the kingpin may be on top of the closed jaws and the trailer could come loose easily
explanation: Step 13 instructs making sure there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; space means the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws and the trailer would come loose very easily.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 13

question: What warning does the manual give in Step 15 (Raise Front Trailer Supports) about landing gear position while driving?
choice_a: Never drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things
choice_b: The landing gear must always remain halfway raised while driving
choice_c: Landing gear position does not matter once the vehicle is coupled
choice_d: The landing gear should be left fully lowered while driving short distances
explanation: Step 15 warns to never drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 15

topic: Uncoupling - easing pressure on locking jaws
question: In Step 2 (Ease Pressure on Locking Jaws) of uncoupling a tractor-semitrailer, what two actions does the manual describe?
choice_a: Raise the landing gear and disconnect the glad hands
choice_b: Shut off the trailer air supply to lock the trailer brakes, then ease pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws by backing up gently
choice_c: Apply the trailer hand valve and drive forward quickly
choice_d: Remove the kingpin manually with a pry bar
explanation: Step 2 of uncoupling instructs shutting off the trailer air supply to lock the trailer brakes, then easing pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws by backing up gently.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.4.2 Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 2

question: According to Step 4 (Lower the Landing Gear) of uncoupling, why does the manual say to crank the landing gear a few extra turns after it makes firm contact with the ground, if the trailer is loaded?
choice_a: To fully lift the trailer off the fifth wheel
choice_b: To engage the trailer's parking brake
choice_c: To lift some weight off the tractor, making it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and easier to couple next time
choice_d: To test whether the landing gear is damaged
explanation: The manual says cranking a few extra turns lifts some weight off the tractor, which makes it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and easier to couple next time.

question: Why does Step 7 (Pull Tractor Partially Clear of Trailer) instruct you to stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer?
choice_a: To keep the glad hands connected longer
choice_b: To allow the ABS system to reset
choice_c: To make it easier to reconnect the electrical cord
choice_d: To prevent the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
explanation: The manual instructs stopping with the tractor frame under the trailer to prevent the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.

question: According to Step 4 (Lock Pintle Hook), how can you tell the pintle hook is correctly locked?

question: What does Step 1 (Park on Level Surface) of the pintle hook uncoupling procedure instruct?

choice_d: Disconnect the safety chains before parking

question: According to Step 3 (Attach Safety Chains) of the gooseneck hitch coupling procedure, what does the manual say about safety chains?

question: In Step 2 of uncoupling a gooseneck hitch, after removing the safety pin and clip and rotating the handle to raise the trailer off the ball, what does the manual say happens to the coupler?

question: During the coupling-system inspection (Figure 6.16), where should the locking jaws be positioned on the kingpin?

question: What does the manual say to check about the landing gear during the walkaround inspection of a combination vehicle?
choice_a: That it is lowered halfway and the crank handle removed
choice_b: That it is fully raised, has no missing parts, is not bent or damaged, and the crank handle is in place and secured
choice_c: That it is painted a reflective color
choice_d: That it has been replaced within the last year

topic: Checking air flows to all trailers
question: How does the manual say to check that air flows to all trailers on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Push in the air supply knob and immediately drive away to feel for brake drag
choice_b: Disconnect the emergency line at the tractor and listen for hissing
choice_c: Push in the red trailer air supply knob, then open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer and listen for escaping air showing the system is charged
choice_d: Apply the parking brake and check the tire pressure gauge
explanation: The manual describes pushing in the red trailer air supply knob, going to the rear of the rig, and opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer to listen for escaping air, confirming the entire system is charged.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.5.2 Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How does the manual say to test the tractor protection valve?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and slam on the brakes
choice_b: Disconnect the trailer entirely and check for air leaks
choice_c: Turn the ABS system off and monitor the malfunction lamp
choice_d: Charge the air brake system, shut the engine off, then step on and off the brake pedal several times to reduce tank pressure — the control should pop out (or move from 'normal' to 'emergency') when pressure falls into the specified range, usually 20 to 45 psi
explanation: The manual's Test Tractor Protection Valve procedure has you charge the system, shut off the engine, and step on and off the brake pedal to reduce air pressure; the control should pop out or switch to 'emergency' within the manufacturer's specified range, usually 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 6 — subsection 6.5.2 Combination Vehicle Brake Check
